4344.dq: Les tons sont fixes: c.-à-d. que les syllables dans les mots ont toujours le même ton. (De Boeck 1952: 9 — a word-level tone statement; no stress or phrase-prominence statement anywhere in the source)
4344.dloc: De Boeck 1952, p. 9, Chapter I 'Phonologie', §3 'La tonologie'. Bokula 1982 §1.10 'La tonalité' pp. 119-120.
4344.prule: No word-stress rule stated. Mondunga/Ndunga is described as a two-tone language (high vs low, no phonemic mid tone) with lexically fixed tone on every syllable of the word; tone changes only in rare, determined contexts. Neither first-hand description (De Boeck 1952; Bokula 1982) mentions stress, accent, intensity or prominence; the only occurrence of 'accent' in De Boeck is 'accent descendant' (p. 42), a falling-tone diacritic, and in Bokula 'l'accent aigu' as the high-tone mark.
4344.quote: 3. La tonologie: Le système tonologique ne possède que deux tons 'simples'; le ton haut et le ton bas. Il n'y a pas de ton moyen avec valeur tonologique. Les tons sont fixes: c.-à-d. que les syllables dans les mots ont toujours le même ton. Ce n'est que dans des cas très rares et bien déterminés qu'une syllable change de ton.
4344.loc: De Boeck 1952, p. 9, Chapter I 'Phonologie', §3 'La tonologie'. Bokula 1982 §1.10 'La tonalité' pp. 119-120.

4344.exq_: Ce n'est que dans des cas très rares et bien déterminés qu'une syllable change de ton. (exception to tone fixity, not to a stress rule; Bokula 1982: 119 similarly 'Les tons sont généralement fixes excepté dans certains cas où ils dépendent du type tonal de l'élément grammatical impliqué dans la phr…
4344.tone: Two simple tones, high and low; no phonemic mid tone (De Boeck 1952: 9). Bokula 1982: 119: 'la langue ndunga ne possède que deux tons simples: haut et bas'... 'seules les voyelles sont porteuses de tons'... 'Les tons sont généralement fixes'. Contour (falling, rising, 'triple') tones on final syllables arise from vowel contraction with suffixes (De Boeck pp. 14-16); nominal suffixes of isolated nouns carry low tone in Ndunga (Bokula 1982: 121). Neither source says anything about stress or accent as a separate prominence system; both are silent rather than denying word stress.

tn.quote: Le système tonologique ne possède que deux tons 'simples’; le ton haut et le ton bas. Il n’y a pas de ton moyen avec valeur tonologique. Les tons sont fixes: c.-à-d. que les syllables dans les mots ont toujours le même ton. ... Le radical des noms peut revêtir toutes les mélodies possibles, notamment: haut-haut, haut-bas, bas-bas, bas-haut, pour les radicaux à deux syllabes; etc. Si un radical à type tonologique haut-haut ou bas-haut possède un suffixe du type V, le nom a la mélodie haut-descendant ou bas-descendant
tn.translation: The tonological system has only two 'simple' tones; the high tone and the low tone. There is no mid tone with tonological value. The tones are fixed: i.e. the syllables in words always have the same tone. ... The noun radical can carry all possible melodies, namely: high-high, high-low, low-low, low-high, for two-syllable radicals; etc. If a radical of tonological type high-high or low-high has a suffix of type V, the noun has the melody high-falling or low-falling
tn.cite: De Boeck, L.-B. (1952). Grammaire du Mondunga (Lisala, Congo Belge). Mémoires IRCB, Sci. Morales et Politiques, in-8°, T. XXIV fasc. 2. Bruxelles: IRCB. 60 pp.
tn.locator: p. 9, ch. I §3 'La tonologie'... p. 16, ch. II §3 'La tonologie des noms'
tn.note: Two level tones, high and low, lexically fixed on each syllable; falling, rising and 'triple' tones on word-final vowels come from contraction with the low-toned noun suffix. Stress not mentioned.

4344.cfw: De Boeck's 1952 grammar and Bokula's 1982 comparative study, the only first-hand descriptions of Mondunga, both give it two fixed tones (high and low) and say nothing of word stress, and Tucker and Bryan's 1966 survey agrees on the two lexical tones while adding only a hedged, group-level remark that stress 'seems to fall' on the first syllable of the stem, so the tonal reading rests on few but concordant sources.

4345.prule: Penultimate accent is the stated unmarked position: 'accent, indien niet aangegeven, op voorlaatste lettergreep' (accent, where not indicated, on the penultimate syllable). Items whose accent falls elsewhere carry a written acute in the list: final tiontión 'cough', pomí 'I', patajá 'village', kanawa alampé 'landing place'; antepenult/initial mékolo 'black man', pákolo 'house', trángamee, báraba 'beard' (pp. 204-205); a few penult items carry a redundant acute (e.g. wákoe, p. 204). Weight, vowel quality and morphology are never mentioned as conditions; the deviations are given item by item. scan of the part-A list shows 68 acute-bearing tokens, about 43 distinct spellings, over about 329 entry lines, and the scan drops some acutes (p. 204's tiontión, pomí, bárba, wákoe are not captured), so the marked minority is somewhat larger than that count; neither reader nor the adjudicator counted in full.

4346.prule: Accent position is lexically determined: syllables are underlyingly marked or unmarked, at most one marked syllable per morpheme, and the marking is contrastive (tsifungú 'j'ai fermé' vs rifúngu 'nous avons fermé'; tsilátsa vs rílatsa, pp. 274-275). Feet are built post-lexically over the prosodic group: final syllable extrametrical unless marked, unbounded left-headed feet, an H on the last syllable of each foot, all H but the first of the group deleted. In a word in isolation the H therefore surfaces on the marked syllable (or, with two marked syllables in the group, on the syllable before the second marked one, e.g. tsionó wana wararu). No weight conditioning is mentioned.
4346.srule: None: one accent (H) per prosodic group -- 'les H sont tous effacés à l'exception du premier du groupe' (p. 351), 'seul le premier H d'un groupe demeure' (p. 510); non-initial feet keep no surface prominence and no secondary or rhythmic accent is described.

4346.tone: Accent is realised as a single H per prosodic group (accented syllable high, following syllables associate to the H in neutral intonation, pp. 355-356). Philippson explicitly rejects the label 'accent tonal' for 'accent' (pp. 43-44: 'Je propose donc d'abandonner la dénomination d'"accent tonal" au profit de celle, phonologique, d'"accent"') and groups Comorian with Russian (p. 43); his 2005 paper title calls it 'pitch accent'. Rombi 1983: 63 (Shimaore monograph, second-hand) calls the Ndzuani tone system 'assez dégradé'. tone or pitch accent is the defensible alternative verdict.

4348.heavy: Two attractors: (i) 'closed ended' words, i.e. words ending in a consonant (sec. 3.10's own wording; sec. 3.8 defines 'closed syllable ends in a consonant' and lists /pa-har/, /di-mak/, /b∂r-kun/, /dis-tik/ as closed disyllables and /ma-nu/, /un-no-ti/ as open, though it also files vowel-final /d∂r-ka-ri/ 'important' under 'Closed triyliabic words', so the 3.8 labelling is not a clean word-final criterion), whose di- and trisyllables stress 'second syllable' (/de'gar/, /mi'nistar/); (ii) 'where there is a diphthong in a word, the primary stress falls on the diphthong' (/'poila/, /'gutei/). CVV here means diphthong only: six short vowels i e ∂ a o u (sec. 3.1; the thesis's ∂ = 'half close central unrounded', i.e. a schwa /ə/), seven diphthongs that each 'form a single syllable' (sec. 3.4), and no vowel-length contrast reported anywhere in ch. 3.

4351.prule: Stress (the 'strong' or 'stressed' syllable) is morphologically assigned: it falls on the stem-initial syllable. In unprefixed words, including suffixed words, that is the first syllable; after the negative prefix ma- it is the second syllable (the stem's first); in compounds and numeral-classifier constructions the initial syllable of each stem is strong. It is non-contrastive ('not linguistically significant at the word-level', Kansakar 1977:1) and is used by these authors chiefly as the conditioning environment for vowel and glide allophony.
4351.srule: No secondary or rhythmic stress described. Only multi-stem words carry more than one strong syllable: in compounds and numeral + classifier constructions the initial syllable of each stem is strong (e.g. /pe-kaa/ 'four times', classifier word-final but strong), with neither ranked as secondary; Kansakar 1980:15 /bye-koo/ 'bent' has a weak first and a strong second syllable, i.e. a single strong syllable that is not word-initial; single-stem words have one strong syllable, the rest weak.

4354.dq: As to accent, I sometimes found the last syllable of a word had an emphasis on it, and it was in a rising tone.
4354.dloc: p. 241, 'NOTE' following the pronoun table, fifth paragraph (the only prosodic remark in the article)
4354.prule: none stated: an impressionistic report that the final syllable of a word 'sometimes' carried emphasis together with a rising pitch; no rule, no contrast, no marked examples
4354.quote: As to accent, I sometimes found the last syllable of a word had an emphasis on it, and it was in a rising tone.
4354.loc: p. 241, 'NOTE' following the pronoun table, fifth paragraph (the only prosodic remark in the article); identity passage p. 234
4354.idn: the old language of Ngala (Ngala Language); the town's present language is Kanuri; data: Ngala town, 'about twenty-eight miles north-north-east of Dikwa on the south side of Lake Chad' (Bornu); wordlist dictated by the two last old male speakers Ladan Braima (c. 81) and Mahman Tahir (73), ages reckoned as of 1922
4354.exq_: As to accent, I sometimes found the last syllable of a word had an emphasis on it, and it was in a rising tone.
4354.tone: Migeod says the emphasised final syllable 'was in a rising tone' (p. 241); he describes no tone system, and the wordlist (pp. 236-241) carries no tone or accent marks (no acute/grave marks; only stray circumflex/breve-like marks on a few vowels, e.g. 'Tum', 'Mum', p. 238). Migeod's own affiliation statement (p. 234: 'The old language of Ngala was related to the Makari farther east') and Glottolog's language comment ('Kotoko group of Chadic, closest to Makari (= Mpade)') place it next to Mpade/Makary Kotoko, a five-tone language (Allison 2012 p. 26); the other northern-Kotoko neighbour Malgbe/Goulfey is likewise tonal (Tourneux 2003 §1.3 'Touchant les tons', forms tone-marked). So the 'rising tone' remark is as compatible with lexical tone (the family norm) or with citation-list intonation as with word stress.

4355.dq: Certain words seem to always carry a stress (on the first vowel); /ndāà/, /dēę̀/.
4355.dloc: A Grammatical Sketch of Sara-Ngambay, I. 'Phonology Structure' / 'La structure phonologique', section C. Stress / C. L'accent, p. 24 (also stamped G-7); IA leaf index 24 (page)
4355.prule: No stress rule. Sara-Ngambay is a three-register-tone language (H/M/L; every vowel and nasal carries its own tone). The authors do not mark stress, say its status (grammatical vs lexical) 'remains to be discovered', and record only a hedged observation that certain words with a mid+low vowel sequence (/ndāà/ 'and then', /dēę̀/ 'they') seem always to carry a stress on their first vowel, heard as the mid tone raised to high.
4355.srule: Not mentioned in Thayer & Thayer 1971, vol. 3, Part I §C 'Stress' (p. 24; whole phonology part pp. 22-25 and the tone-tendency remarks p. 69 read): the source gives no secondary, rhythmic or non-primary stress information; its only stress statement is that stress is unmarked, its grammatical-vs-lexical status undiscovered, and that certain words seem to carry a first-vowel stress.
4355.quote: C. Stress. We do not mark stress anywhere in the texts. Whether it is grammatical or lexical remains to be discovered. Certain words seem to always carry a stress (on the first vowel); /ndāà/, /dēę̀/. This makes them sound as if the mid tone is raised to high: /ndáà/, /déę̀/.
4355.loc: A Grammatical Sketch of Sara-Ngambay, I. 'Phonology Structure' / 'La structure phonologique', section C. Stress / C. L'accent, p. 24 (also stamped G-7); IA leaf index 24 (page)
4355.idn: Sara-Ngambay (Ngambay) as spoken in the town of Moundou, southern Chad ('taken as standard'); data: Six months of fieldwork in Chad (prefaces dated February and June 1971) with Mr. Noé Kyambé and Mr. Adoum Eloi Gondjé as 'language teachers and linguistic informants'; Vol. 1 Introduction C 'Production of the manual'…
4355.exq_: Whether it is grammatical or lexical remains to be discovered.
4355.tone: Same page, section B (English column): 'B. Tone. Each vowel and nasal has its own tone. Nasals are always mid tone. When two adjacent vowels are within the same morpheme, the first is mid, the second high or low.' Long vowel = two identical vowels with tones following that rule. Stress: unmarked in the texts; grammatical-vs-lexical status explicitly unknown; only observation is first-vowel prominence on some M+L VV words, perceived as M raised to H. The only other stress mention is p. 69 (VI. Phonological Processes, ii): in a /M H H H M/ string the second H 'might become higher than the first and third /H/, if there were emphasis, stress, or something else to raise the general pitch level' - given 'not to formulate rules from them, but rather to illustrate certain tendencies'. The 2010 GIALens sketch (Ndjerareou, Melick & Moeller) states three contrastive register tones H/M/L and never uses the words stress or accent.

4356.dq: les tons apparaissent dans les mots de manière entièrement imprévisibles (tone is described at word level; no stress domain of any kind is stated)
4356.prule: No stress or accent rule stated. Ngam is described as a three-level tone language (high, mid, low; §1.4.1.2) with eight further complex/modulated tones (§1.4.1.3); tone is lexically 'entièrement imprévisible' and is the only prosodic feature the phonology treats.
4356.quote: Le ton est donc un trait prosodique important. A part l'uniformité tonale constatée dans la majorité des mots de la catégorie adjectivale (ton bas lorsqu'ils sont isolés), les tons apparaissent dans les mots de manière entièrement imprévisibles. Signalons cependant que, lorsque le mot est monosyllabique, la plupart des tons utilisés sont des tons simples bas, moyen ou haut, ce qui permet d'avoir un nombre assez élevé de paires minimales tonales en opposant les mots de ce type. [...] 1.4.1.2. Les tons simples. La langue possède trois tons simples: le ton haut, le ton moyen et le ton bas qui so…
4356.idn: ngam, variante tra (/t[a/) — the author's own name for the variety studied (a named variety of the language); data: Fieldwork at Sarh (Chad) with speakers brought from Maro, Moyo and Danamadji (plus one living at Mousdan), other informants met at Moyo, Danamadji, Sarh and N'Djamena; five named permanent informants…
4356.exq_: A part l'uniformité tonale constatée dans la majorité des mots de la catégorie adjectivale (ton bas lorsqu'ils sont isolés) (a tonal, not a stress, exception)
4356.tone: Three simple tones H/M/L (p. 77) plus eight complex tones (p. 78); tone rules: mid tone blocks doubling of another tone, high tone modulates or raises a following low, locative high tone combines with any word-final tone, low tone marks interrogation (§1.4.1.1, §1.4.4). The whole 348-page thesis has no technical use of accent/accentuation/intensité/proéminence/stress (the full-text search hits are all 'mettre l'accent sur', 'figement accentué', 'faible intensité'). Keegan 2014, The Eastern Sara Languages, p. 9: 'All of the Sara Languages have three even tones: high, mid and low'; Keegan's Ngam lexicon marks tone on every vowel and says nothing about stress.

tn.quote: La langue possède trois tons simples: le ton haut, le ton moyen et le ton bas qui sont respectivement représentés par les symboles: ´ ¯ ` . Phonétiquement, ces tons sont très distincts les uns des autres et se perçoivent sans difficulté. ... La langue atteste huit tons complexes qui correspondent à des combinaisons de tons simples. Les deux derniers sont les tons descendant et ascendant.

Phonetically these tones are very distinct from one another and are perceived without difficulty. ... The language attests eight complex tones which correspond to combinations of simple tones. The modulated tones are sets of two different simple tones carried by successive vowels of the same quality within one word. ... The last two are the falling and rising tones.

4359.tone: Halme 2004 (secondary) reports Baucom 1972: all Wambo languages employ two tone phonemes; the Wambo varieties differ from each other mostly in tone; much tonal variation from one variety to the next (Baucom 1972:53). Halme has tonal data for only four of the twelve varieties (Kwanyama, Mbandja, Ndonga, Mbalanhu), so she has no Ngandjera data of her own; Ngandjera is covered only by Baucom's cluster-wide statement, which lists it by name. Lexical tone only; nothing is said about word- or phrase-level stress or accent for Ngandjera. The fragment 'the default place of the accent (der Ton) being the penultimate syllable' in the same section is Halme summarising an early German grammar of Kwanyama, not Ngandjera, and is excluded. The 'tonal variation' sentence quoted under 'Exceptions' is a caveat on cross-variety tone, not an exception to a stress rule (none is given).

4362.dloc: SPA 1979 vol. 1, entry 015 Angas, PAGE 010, entry '$a STRESS', quoting Burquest 1971 p. 9.
4362.prule: No stress-placement rule stated. Burquest 1971 (via SPA 1979): each phonological word carries exactly one stress, which is non-phonemic and not used for emphasis, and whose conditioning factors 'have not yet been fully studied'. The language has three level tones high/mid/low (with falling and rising allotones; 'domain of tone: syllable'); Jungraithmayr & Holubova 2016 (via Tourneux 2016) give three registers H/B/M with lexical and demarcative function. Words are overwhelmingly monosyllabic (Foulkes 1915: 1; Tourneux 2016).

4362.tone: Three level tones: SPA 1979 items 81 high ([high-falling] allotone), 82 mid, 83 low ([low-rising] allotone), 'domain of tone: syllable', sentence-level downdrift (INTONATION entry), from Burquest 1971 pp. 8, 17-18; PHOIBLE SPA 125 lists the same three tone levels. J&H 2016 via Tourneux 2016: 'On a trois registres tonals (H, B, M) et les tons ponctuels et modules qui en decoulent. Le ton a une fonction lexicale et demarcative.' What the sources say about stress/accent: Burquest (via SPA) posits one non-phonemic stress per phonological word with unstudied conditioning; SPA footnotes 60 and 72 (Burquest pp. 37, 8) refer to 'the onset slot of unstressed syllables' and an echo vowel 'utterance finally after stressed consonant final syllables', so stress is a real but undescribed prominence in his analysis. Foulkes 1915 marks 'accentuation' with an acute on individual words and phrases (p. ix), denies that 'intonation' (tone) is a feature (p. 1) but concedes es 'egg/flour' and nyin 'hunger/tired' differ by 'intonation high/low' (vocabulary notes); his acutes are most plausibly high-tone marks. Tourneux 2016 para. 5 reports J&H 2016 calling the final CC syllable of CV-r/lC disyllables 'non accentuee' (second-hand; no rule).

4363.dq: In Mankon we find that Leroy's super high tone does not originate from a falling tone neither can it be said to have developed from any kind of stress pattern since Mankon does not seem to be a stress accent language.
4363.dloc: Chapter Twenty-two 'Mankon Tone', sec. 22.5 (review of Leroy 1977), pp. 393-395; first sentence spans bottom of p. 393 to top of p. 394, second sentence is on p. 395 (not p. 394 as the two compilers said).
4363.prule: Tone language (underlying H/L; surface H, M, L with downstep and floating tones per Mfonyam ch. 22; Leroy 1977 adds a disputed super-high tone). The only stress statement is a hedged denial: Mankon 'does not seem to be a stress accent language' and the super-high tone 'is not related to any stress pattern in Mankon either'. No word-stress position is stated in any opened source.
4363.srule: Not mentioned in Mfonyam 1989, ch. 22 'Mankon Tone' (pp. 373-400 read in full): the chapter describes tone only; its two stress remarks (pp. 394-395) deny that Mankon is a stress-accent language and give no stress placement, primary or secondary.
4363.quote: Although in some of the languages where extra H tone exists, its realization is related to a falling tone, its realization in Mankon, by Leroy's description, is different or rather unique. Faraclas (1984:14), who recognizes a similar tone in Obolo, says that the extra H tone in Obolo comes from two sources: "lexically it is derived from a falling tone, while grammatically, it has developed as the result of stress patterns in the language." In Mankon we find that Leroy's super high tone does not originate from a falling tone neither can it be said to have developed from any kind of stress patt…
4363.loc: Chapter Twenty-two 'Mankon Tone', sec. 22.5 (review of Leroy 1977), pp. 393-395; first sentence spans bottom of p. 393 to top of p. 394, second sentence is on p. 395 (not p. 394 as the two compilers said).
4363.idn: Mankon (Grassfields Bantu, Ngemba subgroup, North West Province of Cameroon); tone data largely cited from Leroy 1977 and checked against the author's own informant (a named variety of the language); data: the author's Mankon informant was Mr. Frederick Fon, who 'lives in Alabukam, Mankon village but works in Bamenda' (notes to ch. 22, n. 1, p. 400); a 'different informant' supplied data for a preliminary instrumental check (p. 396); dates not stated in ch. 22. The chapter takes its examples from Leroy (1977:70-74)…
4363.exq_: since Mankon does not seem to be a stress accent language
4363.tone: Mankon is a tone language: Mfonyam 1989 ch. 22 analyses H, M, L surface tones from underlying H/L with downstep (T-rule 2) and rejects Leroy's super-high tone; Warnier & Voorhoeve 1975 pp. 129-134: L/H on each vowel, upstep/downstep; Swiri 1998 sec. 4.2.2 p. 73: 'The Mankon language being an African language is no exception for being a tone language. Loan-words from these stress-timed languages are compelled to bear tones. H tones are marked where syllables bearing primary stress are borrowed. The unstressed syllable bears L or M tones.' On stress/accent the sources say only that Mankon 'does not seem to be a stress accent language' (Mfonyam p. 394) and that the super-high tone 'is not related to any stress pattern in Mankon either' (p. 395).

4365.dq: This happens because the first syllable of roots in Ngiemboon is always stressed, the second syllable and any suffix is always unstressed. (Anderson 2008 §4.4) ... This means that all noun and verb prefixes and any second syllables on the roots are unstressed. (Anderson 2001 §6.1)
4365.dloc: Primary: Anderson 2008 p. 5, §4.4 '“Echo vowels”'. Secondary: Anderson 2001 §6 'Stress', §6.1 'Nouns and Verbs: First syllable of root', §6.2 'Functors', all on p. 47 (p. 48 begins inside §7 'Tone'); scope statement ('all examples in this paper will be from that language unless otherwise noted') p. 33, §1 Introduction.
4365.prule: Stress falls on the first syllable of the root; the root's second syllable and any suffix (/-te/ or a vowel) are always unstressed (Anderson 2008 §4.4). Position is fixed relative to the root, not to the word: prefixes (a vowel or a syllabic homorganic nasal, 2008 §2.1) precede the root and are not mentioned in the 2008 statement, but Anderson 2001 §6.1 states explicitly that 'all noun and verb prefixes and any second syllables on the roots are unstressed', so the stressed syllable is word-initial in prefixless words and word-second in prefixed words such as [ŋ̩́kjɛ́] 'to jump' (2008 §3). No syllable-count grid can be written because prefix presence varies.
4365.srule: Secondary stress is not mentioned in either source (Anderson 2008 §4.4; Anderson 2001 §6-6.2): only the root-initial syllable is described as stressed, with prefixes, root-second syllables and suffixes unstressed.

4365.tone: Tone language. Anderson 2008 §6 'Tone': Ngiemboon and other Eastern Grassfields Bantu languages are known 'for the complexity of their tone systems'; 'it is underlying, lexical, word-level tone that is written'; §6.1 four main tone melodies on noun stems (rising, downstepped high, low, low-falling); verb roots contrast only H and L with 'a very high number of verb roots that are members of tone minimal pairs'; §6.2 floating TAM tones perturb conjugated verbs (details referred to Anderson 1983). 4367.tone: Three contrastive tones in unchecked syllables, Figure 9 (p. 22): '54 high' with allotones 54 (53) 5 45 4; '3 mid' with allotones 3 32; '31 mid falling' with allotones 32 31. The prose on p. 22 adds a 43 realisation of the mid tone: 'In the mid tone examples the contour 43 and level 3 are predominant. There are contour tones of 32, however.' Checked syllables carry a high vs low register: 'The high register is found in checked syllables with a 5 or 43. The low register is found in checked syllables with 3, 32 and 31 tones.' (p. 23). 'Tone is found to be unpredictable in unchecked syllables while predictable in checked syllables.' (p. 21). Register in checked syllables correlates with onset voicing: 'In high register tones the onset is voiceless while in low register tones the onset is voiced. This is seen as a more general pattern because counter examples can be found with the words, east, ring, turtle, etc.' (p. 24). On stress the source says only that the full syllable types are stressed and tone-bearing ('The tone is obligatory in stressed syllables', p. 9; 'there are no stressed syllables of the *V(C) type', p. 9) and that the presyllable is unstressed and often schwa (p. 8); stress itself is explicitly outside the study (p. 7 fn. 6). No pitch-accent analysis; no placement rule for strings of full syllables.

Lingombe has four tones. - two simple tones: a low tone (\), which for economy is represented in writing by the absence of a sign, and a high tone (´). dalá (walk) / dala (rubbish bin) njilí (blows) / njili (palm grove) ... - two double tones: a rising (ˇ) and a falling (ˆ) mǎ (spear) / mâ (mother) mosɔ̌ (sugar-cane shoot) / mosɔ̂ (quarrel) ... The tone characterises each syllable of the word and is carried by the vowel, its most evident part.
